name: Dooars and the Terai
tagline: Rhino grass, tea lines and the doors to Bhutan
meta_description: Plan the Dooars on a fair budget: Siliguri arrivals, Gorumara and Jaldapara safaris, forest lodges, Buxa Fort, tea gardens and true local stories.
summary: The Dooars are the forested plains at the foot of the hills, from the Teesta to the Sankosh. Fly into Bagdogra or take a train to NJP, then spend two to four nights at Lataguri and Madarihat for Gorumara and Jaldapara. Go October to May; the parks shut from mid-June to mid-September.
intro: Most people meet the Dooars by accident. They land at Bagdogra or step off a train at New Jalpaiguri, take a jeep straight up to Darjeeling or Gangtok, and never look east. That is a pity, because two hours from Siliguri the road crosses the Teesta at the Coronation Bridge and drops into a different country: tall elephant grass, sal forest, rivers of white stones and tea gardens that run for kilometres. This is where you see a one-horned rhino from a jeep at dawn, eat river fish with rice in a roadside hotel, and sleep in a forest lodge that costs less than a city hotel.

The name comes from the old word for doors. Eighteen passes once led from these plains up into Bhutan, and for two centuries the Bhutanese governed much of this strip. The British took it after the Duar War of 1864–65, cleared the forest for tea from the 1870s, and brought in workers from the Chota Nagpur plateau whose grandchildren still live in the garden lines. Rajbanshi farmers, Mech and Rabha villages, Nepali settlers and the small Toto community at Totopara all share this land. You hear Bengali, Rajbanshi, Nepali and Sadri in a single market.

For planning, think of the Dooars in three belts. The western belt, around Lataguri, Murti, Chalsa and Samsing, is one to two hours from Siliguri and holds Gorumara National Park, the Chapramari forest and the rivers that tumble out of the Neora Valley. The central belt around Madarihat and Hasimara is Jaldapara country, home to the second-largest population of one-horned rhinos in India, with Chilapata and Totopara next door. The eastern belt is Buxa Tiger Reserve, Jayanti and the old Buxa Fort on the Bhutan border.

The Dooars are the cheapest wildlife holiday in eastern India if you plan well. Government forest and tourism lodges charge ₹1,500–4,000 a night, a shared safari jeep splits six ways, and buses and local trains connect most towns. Where people overspend is on last-minute safari tickets bought from touts, on a reserved car for days when they do not move, and on peak Puja and Christmas weeks. This section of the site tells you how to avoid all three, and what is worth paying for.

story.title: Eighteen doors and the war that closed them
paras: Look at a map of the foothills between the Teesta and the Manas and you can still trace the old passes: Buxa, Bala, Chamurchi and others, each a river gap where traders came down from Bhutan. The word duar, or dooar, means door in Bengali and Assamese, and there were eighteen of them. Through these doors came wool, rock salt, musk and ponies from the hills, and down here went rice, dried fish and silk. By the eighteenth century Bhutan ruled most of the plains west of the Sankosh through its regional governors, the penlops, and their local officers.

In 1863 the British sent Ashley Eden to Punakha to settle border raids and the return of captives. The mission went badly; Eden later said he had been forced to sign a treaty under pressure, and the British disowned it. In late 1864 four columns of the Duar Field Force marched into the foothills. Buxa and the western passes fell quickly; at Dewangiri in the east the Bhutanese drove a British garrison out before it was retaken in 1865. The war was short, wet and costly for both sides.

On 11 November 1865 the Treaty of Sinchula ended it. Bhutan ceded the Eighteen Duars and a strip of hill territory east of the Teesta, around a fifth of its land, in return for an annual allowance that rose to ₹50,000. Within ten years the first tea garden of the Dooars was opened at Gazaldoba, and by 1881 there were 55. The forests you drive through today, the tea lines, the railway and even the district boundaries all trace back to that treaty.

did_you_know: Duar means door: eighteen passes once led from these plains up into Bhutan, which is where the name Dooars comes from.
Jaldapara had only 14 one-horned rhinos in 1985; the March 2025 census estimated 331 there and 61 in Gorumara.
The Coronation Bridge over the Teesta at Sevoke was begun in 1937 to mark the coronation of George VI and finished in 1941.
Buxa Fort, a Bhutanese frontier post taken by the British, was used as a detention camp for Indian freedom fighters in the 1930s.
The Toto language of Totopara got its own script, created by community elder Dhaniram Toto, which entered the Unicode Standard in 2021.

highlights.title: Rhinos at Jaldapara at dawn
highlights.text: A 6 a.m. jeep through the Torsa grasslands is the best chance in Bengal to see a one-horned rhino grazing in the open. Jaldapara holds about 331 of them by the 2025 count, and morning slots sell out first in winter weekends.

highlights.title: Gorumara's watchtowers
highlights.text: Instead of chasing animals, you sit. Jatraprasad, Chukchuki, Chandrachur and Medla towers look over salt licks and water holes where gaur, elephant, peafowl and rhino come out. Each slot is about 90 minutes and costs a few hundred rupees per person.

highlights.title: Forest lodges under ₹3,000
highlights.text: The forest and tourism corporations run lodges at Murti, Lataguri, Madarihat and the Kodalbasti edge of Chilapata. Rooms are plain, food is home-style, and you hear the forest at night for the price of a city guest house.

highlights.title: Buxa Fort and Lepchakha
highlights.text: A one-hour climb from Santalabari leads to the ruins of Buxa Fort, a Bhutanese outpost that became a British jail for freedom fighters. Half an hour higher, the Drukpa village of Lepchakha looks over the rivers of the Dooars.

highlights.title: Tea country on foot
highlights.text: From Chalsa to Hasimara the road runs between tea gardens planted from the 1870s. Morning walks along garden roads, a cup of strong CTC at a roadside stall and the Karam festival in late summer show the Adivasi side of tea.

highlights.title: Rivers out of the hills
highlights.text: The Murti, Jaldhaka and Suntale Khola come out of the hills clear and cold. Rocky Island near Samsing, the Jaldhaka at Jhalong and the barrage at Bindu make easy half-days, and in winter you can sit on the stones all afternoon.

getting_there: Everything starts at Siliguri. Bagdogra Airport (IXB) is about 14 km from the city, with direct flights from Kolkata, Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Chennai and other cities. New Jalpaiguri (NJP) is the main railway station, with overnight trains from Kolkata such as the Darjeeling Mail and Padatik Express and the daytime Vande Bharat from Howrah. For the Dooars you can also stay on the train: the Kanchankanya Express from Sealdah runs through New Mal Junction, Chalsa and Hasimara on its way to Alipurduar. From Siliguri, buses and shared vehicles run along the NH17 corridor via Sevoke and Malbazar to Lataguri in about 2–2.5 hours, and on to Madarihat for Jaldapara in 3–3.5 hours. A reserved car is the easiest way to link several parks.
permits: Indian citizens need no permit to travel in the Dooars. Entry into Gorumara, Jaldapara, Chapramari, Chilapata, Buxa and Mahananda is by safari or watchtower ticket, sold online by the forest department and at park counters; carry photo ID that matches the booking. The Buxa Fort and Jayanti treks need a forest entry ticket and are best done with a local guide. Crossing into Bhutan at Jaigaon–Phuentsholing needs a permit issued at the Phuentsholing immigration office; Indians use a passport or voter ID and pay Bhutan's Sustainable Development Fee, while other nationals need a visa arranged in advance. Rules change, so check current status before you travel.

budget.summary: The Dooars reward people who plan a week ahead. Book safari slots yourself as soon as booking opens, stay in a government forest or tourism lodge rather than a resort, and pick one base per park so you are not paying a car to sit idle. Travel by train to New Mal or Hasimara instead of paying for a long road transfer from Siliguri. Avoid the Durga Puja week and 24 December to 1 January, when rooms double and safari slots vanish.
costs: Shared jeep or bus Siliguri → Lataguri
Day hire of a car for local sightseeing
tips: Book safari tickets on the official forest department portal or at the park counter, never from a stranger at the gate who offers seats at double price.
Share a safari jeep: the price is per vehicle, so six people pay a sixth each.
Watchtower sessions at Gorumara cost far less than a full jeep safari and often show more animals.
Take the Kanchankanya Express or a local train along the Dooars line instead of hiring a car for long transfers.
Mid-week stays in November, February and March cost 20–40% less than weekends and holidays at most lodges.

months.summary: January is cool and dry, with thick fog until 9 a.m. on many days and bright afternoons. Grassland is still tall, so rhinos can be hard to see on some routes, but birding is at its peak: migrant ducks on the Teesta at Gajoldoba, and forest birds at Buxa and Chapramari. Nights in forest lodges are cold, so pack a warm layer. After New Year week, crowds thin and rooms are easy.
months.tip: Book the afternoon safari rather than the first dawn slot if fog is forecast; you will see more.
months.price_note: Rates fall back to normal after the first week; weekdays are the best value of the winter.

months.summary: One of the best months. Days are warm, mornings crisp and the forest department begins controlled burning of old grass, which opens views for rhino and gaur. The sal is in fresh leaf. Mahashivratri brings the Jalpesh fair near Maynaguri when it falls in February. A good month for the Buxa Fort climb and Jayanti riverbed walks before the heat sets in.
months.tip: Pair a Gorumara watchtower afternoon with a Jaldapara dawn jeep for the best rhino odds.
months.price_note: Normal season rates; weekends near Valentine's and long weekends fill fast at Lataguri.

months.summary: Grass is short after burning and animals come to water in the open, which makes March the strongest month for sightings at Jaldapara and Gorumara. Afternoons turn warm and hazy, so do your safaris early and rest at noon. Holi week sees family groups from Kolkata. Jalpesh Mela is held at Shivaratri if it falls in early March.
months.tip: Carry water and a cap on watchtowers; there is little shade by 10 a.m.
months.price_note: Prices are steady; Holi week and school holidays push weekend rates up.

months.summary: Hot and humid, with pre-monsoon thunderstorms in the evenings. Sightings remain good because water is scarce and animals stay near water holes. Fewer tourists come, so lodges are quiet. Bengali New Year (Poila Baisakh) in mid-April brings fairs in towns. River spots like Rocky Island and Jhalong are pleasant in the early morning.
months.tip: Book a room with a fan or AC and take safaris at 6 a.m. or after 3:30 p.m.
months.price_note: Shoulder season: many private resorts offer mid-week discounts.

months.summary: The last month before closure. It is sticky and storms arrive most afternoons, but parks run and crowds are small. Summer holidays bring families from Kolkata and Dhaka in the second half of the month. Plan forest days for dawn and use the heat of the day for travel or rest. Leeches appear on forest walks after rain.
months.tip: Combine the Dooars with two nights in Darjeeling or Lava to escape the afternoon heat.
months.price_note: School holiday weekends are busy; mid-week rooms are cheap.

months.summary: The monsoon arrives in early June. National parks and sanctuaries close from 16 June to 15 September for the breeding season and because forest roads wash out. Before the 15th, safaris still run in wet conditions. After that, the Dooars are best seen from the train window: tea gardens in full green and rivers in spate. Not a month to plan a wildlife trip.
months.tip: If you are passing through Siliguri, the Coronation Bridge and Sevoke river views are at their most dramatic now.
months.price_note: Off season: resorts that stay open cut rates sharply, but most of what you came for is closed.

months.summary: Peak monsoon. Parks are closed, rivers flood, and the road to Totopara and some forest villages can be cut for days. Landslides affect the hill roads to Darjeeling, Kalimpong and Sikkim. Siliguri itself works as normal and is the place to sit out a blocked road. Tea plucking is at its height in the gardens.
months.tip: Do not plan a Dooars wildlife trip in July; come back from October.
months.price_note: Lowest rates of the year at the few properties that stay open.

months.summary: Still closed for wildlife. The Karam festival falls in late August or September in the tea gardens, depending on the lunar date, and is the main reason to be here. Expect heavy showers, washed-out roads and leeches. Siliguri's markets fill up before the Puja season.
months.tip: If you want Karam, stay near Chalsa or Malbazar and ask your host which garden is celebrating that year.
months.price_note: Very cheap where open; advance Puja bookings for October start now.

months.summary: Parks reopen on 16 September, often to deep green forest and full rivers. Grass is very tall, so sightings are patchy, but the first weeks are uncrowded. Rain still falls most days. The Karam festival can fall in early September. From the middle of the month, Siliguri gears up for Durga Puja and hotel rates start to rise.
months.tip: Book safaris only for after reopening day and keep a buffer day for washed-out forest tracks.
months.price_note: Opening weeks are good value; Puja-week rates appear at the end of the month.

months.summary: The season starts properly. Durga Puja fills Siliguri and Jalpaiguri with pandals, and the day after Dashami the Rajbanshi Bhandani Puja is held at Barnish near Maynaguri and across the Dooars. Puja week is the busiest of the year in the parks. Skies clear by the end of the month and the hills show from the plains on good mornings.
months.tip: If your dates are fixed to the Puja holidays, book safari slots the day booking opens.
months.price_note: Puja week is the most expensive week of the year; late October is calmer.

months.summary: Clear, dry and comfortable, and our favourite month. The grass is still high in places but trails are open, rivers drop and the stones of the Murti and Jaldhaka are exposed. Migrant birds start arriving. Kali Puja and Diwali fall in late October or November. A good month for Buxa Fort and Lepchakha, with views to the plains.
months.tip: Pack a light fleece; forest lodges near Buxa and Murti get cold after dark.
months.price_note: Regular rates; the mid-month weeks are quiet and easy to book.

months.weather: Lataguri 10–25 °C, dry, fog later in month
months.summary: Cool, dry and popular. Fog sets in around the solstice and can delay trains into NJP. The Christmas to New Year week is fully booked across Lataguri and Madarihat, with picnic crowds at Rocky Island, Murti and Jhalong. Outside that week, December is excellent for wildlife and birds.
months.tip: Avoid 24 December to 1 January unless you booked months ahead.
months.price_note: Holiday-week rates are the highest after Puja; early December is good value.

faqs.q: When are Gorumara and Jaldapara closed
faqs.a: Both parks, along with Chapramari, Buxa, Chilapata and the other protected forests of the Dooars, close every year from 16 June to 15 September for the monsoon and the breeding season. They reopen on 16 September. Safaris have also generally not run on Thursdays, the weekly closure day. Dates are set each year by the forest department, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days do I need in the Dooars
faqs.a: Two nights at Lataguri cover Gorumara well. Add two nights at Madarihat for Jaldapara and Chilapata, which gives a solid four-night trip. With six to eight nights you can add Buxa Fort and Jayanti, or the rivers at Samsing and Jhalong. Many people tack two nights of Dooars onto a Darjeeling or Gangtok holiday, which works well from Siliguri.

faqs.q: Which is better, Gorumara or Jaldapara
faqs.a: Jaldapara is larger and has far more rhinos, about 331 against Gorumara's 61 in the 2025 census, so your odds of a rhino are better there. Gorumara is closer to Siliguri, has more lodging at Lataguri, and its watchtowers make a relaxed afternoon. If you can, do both: Gorumara first, then Jaldapara, about two hours apart by road.

faqs.q: Is the Dooars safe for families and solo travellers
faqs.a: Yes. Lodges and safaris are run by the forest and tourism departments, and the main towns are used to visitors. Normal care applies: do not walk on forest roads after dark because elephants cross highways, stay inside safari vehicles, and keep children close on watchtowers. Solo women travel here regularly; stay in established lodges and use registered vehicles.

faqs.q: How do I book a Dooars safari
faqs.a: Safaris and watchtower slots are sold by the West Bengal forest department through its online booking portal and at counters in Lataguri and Madarihat. Online slots usually open a set number of days ahead and go quickly on weekends. In autumn 2026 Jaldapara's online booking was down for weeks and only counter tickets were sold, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I do the Dooars by public transport
faqs.a: Mostly, yes. Buses and shared vehicles run from Siliguri to Malbazar, Lataguri, Birpara, Madarihat and Alipurduar, and the Dooars railway line connects New Mal, Chalsa, Nagrakata, Hasimara and Alipurduar. Safaris use forest-registered jeeps that you hire at the gate. You will need a local car only for places like Samsing, Jhalong, Totopara and Santalabari.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit the Dooars
faqs.a: Indian citizens need no permit for the Dooars, only safari or watchtower tickets with matching photo ID. Foreign visitors also need no special permit for the Indian side. If you cross into Bhutan at Jaigaon–Phuentsholing, you need an entry permit from Bhutanese immigration and must pay the Sustainable Development Fee. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Are elephant safaris still offered in the Dooars
faqs.a: Jaldapara has offered elephant-back rides on departmental elephants for decades, and some forest camps have offered them at times. They are contested: animal-welfare groups say riding harms elephants, and rules and availability change from season to season. We do not build trips around them. Jeep safaris and watchtowers give good sightings without riding. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What should I pack for a Dooars safari
faqs.a: Earth-coloured clothes, a warm layer for open jeeps on winter mornings, a cap, sunscreen, water and binoculars. Insect repellent helps in April and May. Carry the ID you used to book. Avoid bright colours and perfume, and do not bring single-use plastic into the parks. A small torch is useful in forest lodges where power can trip during storms.
